text: You now know how to add complex vectors, scale them, and build bases out of them. The one operation missing is the one that actually powers quantum mechanics: a way to multiply two complex vectors together and get a single number back — how much one quantum state overlaps with another.

Physicists write a vector as a ket, psi, and its conjugate transpose — transpose it into a row and conjugate every entry — as a bra, psi. Put a bra next to a ket and you get the inner product, the sum of each conjugated entry of the first vector times the matching entry of the second. That conjugate on the first vector isn't optional — without it, a vector's inner product with itself wouldn't even come out real.

Take psi equals 1 plus i, 2 minus i, and phi equals 3, 1 plus 2i. Conjugating psi's first entry and multiplying by phi's first entry gives 3 minus 3i; the second term works out to 5i. Summing them gives 3 plus 2i — a single complex number out of two complex vectors.

Swap the order and compute phi inner psi instead, and you get 3 minus 2i — the complex conjugate of the first answer. This is a general rule: swapping the order always conjugates the result, which is why the complex inner product isn't symmetric, unlike the real dot product. Setting phi equal to psi itself gives the sum of squared magnitudes — always real and non-negative, exactly what you need to define length. For this psi, that works out to 7, so its norm is the square root of 7.

A Hilbert space is a vector space with this inner product that's also complete — and every finite-dimensional complex vector space, like C squared, qualifies automatically, no extra work required. And here's a first glimpse of where this is heading: if psi and phi are both valid quantum states, the squared magnitude of their inner product is a number between 0 and 1 — a transition probability, the chance of measuring a system prepared in one state and finding it in the other.

Next lesson asks what kind of matrix is allowed to represent something you can actually measure — an energy, a spin, a position — and the answer connects directly to a fact you rely on every day: measurement results are always real numbers.
